B.1: Between now and December seventh, one decision sets what you pay for Medicare all of next year. Medicare has confirmed five changes for twenty twenty-seven, and one of them cuts the price of fifteen popular drugs by up to eighty-five percent.
B.2: Meet Frank and Mary. Frank is sixty-six, on Original Medicare with a drug plan, and he takes a diabetes drug every month. Mary is sixty-eight and has a Medicare Advantage plan. Same street, same mailbox, and two very different letters this fall.
B.3: Every number in this video comes from Medicare and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Let's start with the change that protects you the most if your drugs are expensive.
B.4: Number one is the yearly cap on drug costs. In twenty twenty-six, once you pay two thousand one hundred dollars out of pocket for covered Part D drugs, you pay nothing more for the rest of the year. In twenty twenty-seven, that cap rises to two thousand four hundred dollars.
B.5: The deductible moves too. No Medicare drug plan can have a deductible above seven hundred dollars in twenty twenty-seven, up from six hundred fifteen. Some plans have no deductible at all. That is one of the first things to compare.
B.6: So what does that mean for Frank? If his drugs are expensive, the most he can pay out of pocket for covered drugs next year is two thousand four hundred dollars. That is three hundred dollars more than this year's limit. After that, he pays zero until January.
B.7: And if a big bill early in the year scares you, there is the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan. It spreads your drug costs into monthly payments across the year. Medicare is clear: it does not lower your costs, it only spreads them out.
B.8: Number two is the one Frank cares about. Medicare negotiated the prices of fifteen more brand-name drugs, and those prices take effect on January first, twenty twenty-seven. These drugs treat conditions like diabetes, asthma, cancer and heart disease.
B.9: Here is the biggest one. Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy: the list price for a thirty-day supply was nine hundred fifty-nine dollars. The negotiated price for twenty twenty-seven is two hundred seventy-four. That is seventy-one percent lower.
B.10: And it is not the only one. Trelegy, for asthma and C O P D, goes from six hundred fifty-four dollars to one hundred seventy-five. Janumet, for type two diabetes, goes from five hundred twenty-six to eighty dollars. That is eighty-five percent lower.
B.11: About five point three million people with Medicare used these drugs in twenty twenty-four. Medicare estimates they will save about six hundred eighty-five million dollars out of pocket in twenty twenty-seven.
B.12: But here is the catch. The negotiated price is what your plan pays, not your copay. What you pay still depends on your plan and its drug list. Medicare's own advice is simple: call your plan and ask how these prices affect you.
B.13: Number three is new: the G L P one Bridge. If you have a Medicare drug plan, your plan does not already cover these drugs for you, and you meet the other requirements, you can get certain G L P one drugs for weight loss.
B.14: The cost is a fifty dollar copay for a one-month supply. Not everyone qualifies, so check the rules on medicare dot gov before you count on it. For many people on a fixed income, that is a very different number from the full price.
B.15: Number four is the one most people never check: the premium. For twenty twenty-seven, Medicare says the average Medicare Advantage premium drops from fourteen dollars and thirty-seven cents to twelve dollars a month.
B.16: For a stand-alone drug plan like Frank's, the average premium goes from thirty-five dollars and nine cents to about thirty-six dollars. Less than one dollar more a month, on average. But averages hide a lot.
B.17: Medicare says about eight in ten Advantage members can keep their plan at the same or a lower premium. That also means about two in ten cannot. Mary had to check which group she was in.
B.18: And there is one premium that is not announced yet: Part B. In twenty twenty-six it is two hundred two dollars and ninety cents a month, with a two hundred eighty-three dollar deductible. For most people, it comes straight out of the Social Security check.
B.19: And number five is the trap. Discount cards and coupon sites, like Trump R X, can show a low cash price at the pharmacy. But when you use them instead of your Medicare coverage, that money does not count toward your deductible or your yearly cap.
B.20: So a coupon can save you money today and still leave you further from the two thousand four hundred dollar cap. For a cheap generic, a coupon can make sense. For an expensive drug, using your plan is usually what counts.
B.21: Two more changes worth knowing. Telehealth from your home stays covered through December thirty-first, twenty twenty-seven. And starting in January, Advantage plans can handle prior approvals electronically, so you may see the decision in your patient portal.
B.22: Now the letter. Every fall, your plan mails an Annual Notice of Change. It lists what changes in January: the premium, the deductible, the drug list and the doctors in the network. Most people throw it away without reading it.
B.23: Mary read hers. Her premium stayed the same, but one of her drugs moved to a more expensive tier. That one line would have cost her more every month next year, and she only found it because she opened the letter.
B.24: The dates matter. Open enrollment runs from October fifteenth to December seventh. Any change you make starts on January first. Miss December seventh, and you keep the plan you have, with all its new costs.
B.25: There is one more window. If you are in a Medicare Advantage plan, from January first to March thirty-first you can switch to another Advantage plan, or go back to Original Medicare and add a drug plan.
B.26: So, five changes. One: the drug cap rises to two thousand four hundred dollars. Two: fifteen negotiated drug prices, up to eighty-five percent lower. Three: the G L P one Bridge at fifty dollars. Four: premiums move, and Part B is still coming. Five: coupons do not count toward your cap.
B.27: Three things to do this week. First, open your Annual Notice of Change and circle every number that goes up. Second, put your exact drugs into the Medicare Plan Finder on medicare dot gov. Third, if you are unsure, call your free state SHIP counselor.
B.28: Frank called his plan and confirmed his diabetes drug will cost less in January. Mary used the Plan Finder, switched to a plan that covers her drug on a lower tier, and kept the same doctors. Same street, two smarter years.
